interactions.summary: Jiang extends the problem of Virgil's disappearance, then a student reads Beatrice's stern redirection away from mourning Virgil and toward Dante's next trial.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang interpretation followed by student reading Dante

interactions.summary: Jiang offers one interpretive answer: Virgil leaves because the whole purgatorial journey has disproved his Christian exclusivism and exposed Dante's love for Beatrice as the opposite of Virgil's love logic with Dido.
Jiang concludes that Virgil would rather remain in hell than admit his worldview is wrong, then closes the class by promising to finish the Divine Comedy the following Wednesday.

speaker_notes.note: SPEAKER_00 is still the student reader voicing Beatrice's speech and Dante's narration, not an in-room questioner.
Jiang explicitly frames his account of Virgil's exit as one interpretation among several rather than as a settled doctrinal reading.

claims.claim: Jiang says Virgil's disappearance is strange on multiple practical grounds: Beatrice owes Virgil a favor, Virgil should want to witness Dante's reunion, and ordinary courtesy would suggest handing Dante over directly.
The quoted Beatrice passage tells Dante not to spend his tears on Virgil yet because a harsher wound still lies ahead, effectively shifting his attention away from the guide who just vanished.

Jiang's proposed interpretation is that Virgil remains in hell because he believes he belongs there under a Christian-only salvation framework, even though Dante's poem has already shown cases like Cato that violate that rule.
Jiang says Statius's ascent as a secret Christian provides a second contradiction proving Virgil's framework wrong from within purgatory itself.
Jiang contrasts Dante and Beatrice with Virgil and Dido by saying Dante treats love as giving, sharing, and bestowal, whereas Virgil treats love as receiving, consuming, and controlling.
Jiang interprets Virgil's refusal to witness Dante and Beatrice together as refusal to watch a superior form of love disprove his own worldview.
Jiang closes by saying Virgil would rather burn in hell forever than say 'I am wrong,' and then announces that the class will finish the Divine Comedy the following Wednesday.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture conclusion on 2026-05-22, including a forward schedule note for the next Wednesday session.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice's first move is almost brutal: Virgil is gone, do not waste your tears on him, keep moving toward paradise.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Jiang reads the paradise threshold as a cutting displacement of the old guide rather than a gentle transition.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil is in hell because he is the one still insisting that he belongs there.
signature_moments.source_phrase: No one put him there He should put himself there
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns damnation into a self-imposed fidelity to a broken worldview, which is Jiang's hardest reading of Virgil.

signature_moments.moment: Dante's love gives and keeps giving; Virgil's love takes, consumes, and tries to control.
signature_moments.source_phrase: love Is fundamentally about giving Whereas Virgil believes that love Is fundamentally about receiving And conquering
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's cleanest compression of the Dante-Virgil revolution the whole lecture has been building toward.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil would rather burn forever than admit he was wrong.
signature_moments.source_phrase: He would rather burn in hell For eternity Than to say I am wrong
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the lecture its final psychological thesis about pride, guidance, and why the guide must disappear.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's nameable structure behind Virgil's self-condemnation: only explicit Christians can enter heaven, a rule Dante's poem keeps undoing.
Jiang's characterization of Dante's relation to Beatrice as bestowal and fidelity rather than possession.
Jiang's characterization of Virgil's relation to love, aligned with taking, consuming, and conquest.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-05-22 Jiang explicitly frames Virgil's exit as self-condemnation driven by refusal to surrender a broken worldview; preserve that date if later episodes compare Virgilian guidance, pride, or salvation differently.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang explicitly says this is one interpretation of why Virgil leaves, so the packet preserves the force of the claim without flattening it into an uncontested doctrinal fact.
The 'forget him' phrasing is Jiang's gloss on Beatrice's effect, not a literal stable quotation from the student reading.
